# cliffy

> cliffy generates Python command-line tools from YAML manifests. A manifest lists commands, their params and the Python or shell code each one runs; `cli load` turns it into a CLI (Typer by default, Click with `use_click: true`) that can be tested, documented and built into a single file.

This is the documentation of cliffy 0.7.1, one section per page. Each section starts with a `# <page title>` heading. Source and issues: https://github.com/jaykv/cliffy

<!-- docs/index.md -->

# cliffy


**Describe a command-line tool in YAML. Get a real Python CLI.**

cliffy reads a manifest that lists your commands, their parameters and the code each one runs, and
generates a [Typer](https://typer.tiangolo.com/) application from it. Command bodies are plain Python,
and any line that starts with `$` runs as a shell command, so a manifest can replace a folder of
one-off scripts with a single CLI that has help text, typed arguments and subcommands.

## A CLI in 60 seconds

**1. Install cliffy** (Python 3.11 to 3.15):

```console
$ pip install cliffy
```

**2. Write a manifest** and save it as `hello.yaml`:

```yaml title="hello.yaml"
name: hello
version: 0.1.0
help: Hello world!

commands:
  shell: $ echo "hello from shell"
  python: print("hello from python")
  greet:
    help: Greet someone by name
    params:
      - name: str!
      - --shout|-s: bool = False
    run: |
      message = f"Hello, {name}!"
      print(message.upper() if shout else message)

tests:
  - shell: assert result.exit_code == 0
  - python: assert result.output == "hello from python\n"
  - greet Ada: assert result.output == "Hello, Ada!\n"
  - greet Ada --shout: assert "HELLO, ADA!" in result.output
```

**3. Load it.** cliffy generates the CLI and puts a `hello` command into your Python environment:

```console
$ cli load hello.yaml
✨ Generated hello CLI v0.1.0 ✨
$ hello -h
```

**4. Use it** like any other command:

```console
$ hello shell
hello from shell
$ hello greet Ada --shout
HELLO, ADA!
$ hello --help

 Usage: hello [OPTIONS] COMMAND [ARGS]...

 Hello world!

╭─ Options ──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────╮
│ --version                                                                  │
│ --install-completion          Install completion for the current shell.    │
│ --show-completion             Show completion for the current shell, to    │
│                               copy it or customize the installation.       │
│ --help                -h      Show this message and exit.                  │
╰────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────╯
╭─ Commands ─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────╮
│ shell                                                                      │
│ python                                                                     │
│ greet   Greet someone by name                                              │
╰────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────╯
```

The `tests` section at the bottom of the manifest is optional. `cli test hello.yaml` runs it.

## What you get

- **Python and shell in one place.** Run scripts are Python; lines starting with `$` become
  `subprocess` calls. See [Shell commands](guides/shell-commands.md).
- **Typed parameters with a short syntax.** `name: str!` is a required argument and
  `--count|-c: int = 1` is an option. See [Params and types](guides/params.md).
- **Groups, aliases and templates.** `db.create` nests a command, `delete|rm` adds an alias and
  command templates share params between commands. See
  [Commands, groups and aliases](guides/commands.md).
- **A fast edit loop.** `cli dev` reloads the CLI every time you save the manifest. See
  [Hot-reload dev loop](guides/dev-loop.md).
- **Tests next to the commands.** `cli test` runs the assertions you keep in the manifest. See
  [Testing manifests](guides/testing.md).
- **One file to ship.** `cli build` packs the CLI and its dependencies into a single executable
  zipapp, a single Python script or a native executable. See
  [Building executables](guides/building.md).

## How it works

```text
manifest.yaml ──► validate ──► generate Python (Typer or Click) ──► load │ run │ build
```

1. cliffy renders the manifest with [Jinja2](https://jinja.palletsprojects.com/), parses the YAML and
   validates it against the [manifest schema](reference/manifest.md).
2. It generates one Python module. `cli render` prints that module, so nothing about the result is
   hidden.
3. `cli load` installs the module as a command, `cli run` executes it once and `cli build` packages it.

## Where to go next

| If you want to | Read |
|---|---|
| Install cliffy and its extras | [Installation](installation.md) |
| Build a complete CLI step by step | [Quickstart](quickstart.md) |
| Look up a manifest key | [Manifest reference](reference/manifest.md) |
| Look up a `cli` command or flag | [CLI reference](reference/cli.md) |
| Copy from working manifests | [Examples gallery](reference/examples.md) |
| Upgrade from an older release | [Migration notes](project/migration.md) |

## Similar tools

- [Bashly](https://github.com/DannyBen/bashly) generates Bash CLIs from YAML.
- [Fire](https://github.com/google/python-fire) generates CLIs from Python objects.

<!-- docs/quickstart.md -->

# Quickstart

In this tutorial you build `notes`, a small CLI that stores notes in a JSON file. Along the way you
use every core part of a manifest: commands, params, helper functions, groups, aliases, shell
commands and tests. It takes about 15 minutes.

You need cliffy installed in an active virtual environment. See [Installation](installation.md).

The finished manifest is at the [end of this page](#the-finished-manifest).

## 1. A manifest with one command

Create a file called `notes.yaml`:

```yaml title="notes.yaml"
name: notes
version: 0.1.0
help: Keep short notes in a JSON file

commands:
  add:
    help: Add a note
    params:
      - text: str!
    run: |
      print(f"Added {text}")

tests:
  - add "buy milk": assert result.output == "Added buy milk\n"
```

- `name` is what you will type to run the CLI. `version` is shown by `notes --version`.
- Each key under `commands` is a command. `run` holds its Python code.
- `text: str!` declares a parameter called `text` of type `str`. The `!` makes it required.
  Parameters are ordinary variables inside `run`.
- `tests` is optional. You will come back to it in [step 7](#7-test-it).

Run the command without installing anything:

```console
$ cli run notes.yaml add "buy milk"
Added buy milk
```

`cli run` generates the CLI, runs it once and throws it away. To see the Python it generated, use
`cli render`:

```console
$ cli render notes.yaml
```

```python
def add(text: str = typer.Argument(...)):
    print(f"Added {text}")


cli.command("add", help="Add a note",)(add)
```

Your `run` script became the body of a Typer command function.

## 2. Store the notes

The CLI needs to read and write a file. Add `imports`, `vars` and `functions` between `help` and
`commands`:

```yaml title="notes.yaml"
imports: |
  import json
  import os
  from collections import Counter
  from pathlib import Path

vars:
  default_file: notes.json

functions:
  - |
    def notes_path() -> Path:
        return Path(os.environ.get("NOTES_FILE", "{{ default_file }}"))
  - |
    def load_notes() -> list[dict]:
        path = notes_path()
        return json.loads(path.read_text()) if path.exists() else []
  - |
    def save_notes(notes: list[dict]) -> None:
        notes_path().write_text(json.dumps(notes, indent=2))
```

- `imports` is copied to the top of the generated module.
- `functions` is a list of helper functions that every command can call.
- `vars` defines manifest variables. `{{ default_file }}` is replaced with `notes.json` when the
  manifest is loaded. More in [Vars and Jinja](guides/vars-and-jinja.md).

## 3. Describe parameters once with types

`text: str!` is short, but it has no help text. The `types` section lets you name a full
[Typer parameter definition](https://typer.tiangolo.com/tutorial/arguments/) and reuse it. Add this
after `functions`:

```yaml title="notes.yaml"
types:
  Text: str = typer.Argument(..., help="Text of the note")
  Tag: str = typer.Option("general", "--tag", "-t", help="Tag to file the note under")
```

Now replace the `add` command so that it uses those types and saves the note:

```yaml title="notes.yaml"
commands:
  add:
    help: Add a note
    params:
      - text: Text
      - tag: Tag
    run: |
      notes = load_notes()
      notes.append({"text": text, "tag": tag})
      save_notes(notes)
      print(f"Added note {len(notes)} [{tag}]")
```

Try it:

```console
$ cli run notes.yaml add "buy milk"
Added note 1 [general]
$ cli run notes.yaml -- add "book flights" --tag travel
Added note 2 [travel]
```

!!! tip "The `--` separator"
    When the arguments for your CLI include options such as `--tag`, put `--` after the manifest
    path. Without it, `cli run` tries to interpret `--tag` as one of its own options.

## 4. Add options and an alias

Add a second command under `commands`:

```yaml title="notes.yaml"
  list|ls:
    help: List notes, optionally filtered by tag
    params:
      - --tag|-t: str = ""
    run: |
      for number, note in enumerate(load_notes(), start=1):
          if not tag or note["tag"] == tag:
              print(f"{number}. [{note['tag']}] {note['text']}")
```

- The key `list|ls` creates the command `list` and the alias `ls`.
- `--tag|-t: str = ""` is an option (the name starts with `--`) with the short form `-t` and an
  empty string as its default.

```console
$ cli run notes.yaml list
1. [general] buy milk
2. [travel] book flights
$ cli run notes.yaml -- ls -t travel
2. [travel] book flights
```

## 5. Exit codes and groups

Commands can stop with an error code by raising `typer.Exit`. Add `remove`:

```yaml title="notes.yaml"
  remove|rm:
    help: Remove a note by its number
    params:
      - number: int!
    run: |
      notes = load_notes()
      if not 1 <= number <= len(notes):
          print(f"No note {number}")
          raise typer.Exit(code=1)
      notes.pop(number - 1)
      save_notes(notes)
      print(f"Removed note {number}")
```

A dot in a command key creates a group. These two commands are run as `notes tags list` and
`notes tags rename`. The entry `tags`, which has `help` and no `run`, sets the help text of the group:

```yaml title="notes.yaml"
  tags:
    help: Work with tags

  tags.list:
    help: Count notes per tag
    run: |
      for tag, count in sorted(Counter(note["tag"] for note in load_notes()).items()):
          print(f"{tag} ({count})")

  tags.rename:
    help: Rename a tag on every note
    params:
      - old: str!
      - new: str!
    run: |
      notes = load_notes()
      for note in notes:
          if note["tag"] == old:
              note["tag"] = new
      save_notes(notes)
      print(f"Renamed {old} to {new}")
```

```console
$ cli run notes.yaml tags list
general (1)
travel (1)
$ cli run notes.yaml tags rename general home
Renamed general to home
$ cli run notes.yaml remove 7
No note 7
```

## 6. Call a shell command

A line that starts with `$` is run as a shell command. `f{...}` inserts the value of a Python
expression into it:

```yaml title="notes.yaml"
  backup:
    help: Copy the notes file next to itself
    run: |
      $ cp f{notes_path()} f{notes_path()}.bak
      print(f"Backed up to {notes_path()}.bak")
```

```console
$ cli run notes.yaml backup
Backed up to notes.json.bak
```

More in [Shell commands](guides/shell-commands.md).

## 7. Test it

Replace the `tests` section at the end of the file:

```yaml title="notes.yaml"
tests:
  - $ rm -f notes.json notes.json.bak
  - add "buy milk" --tag home: assert result.output == "Added note 1 [home]\n"
  - add "ship release": assert "Added note 2 [general]" in result.output
  - list: |
      assert "1. [home] buy milk" in result.output
      assert "2. [general] ship release" in result.output
  - ls -t home: assert result_text == "1. [home] buy milk"
  - tags rename general work: assert result.exit_code == 0
  - tags list: assert "work (1)" in result.output
  - backup: assert "Backed up" in result.output
  - remove 9: assert result.exit_code == 1
  - rm 1: assert "Removed note 1" in result.output
  - $ rm -f notes.json notes.json.bak
```

- An entry that starts with `$` is a shell step. Here it removes leftover files before and after
  the run.
- Every other entry maps a command line to Python assertions. `result` is the outcome of the
  command, with `result.output` and `result.exit_code`. `result_text` is the output with
  surrounding whitespace removed.

```console
$ cli test notes.yaml
✨ Invoking tests ✨
...
💚 All tests passed!
```

More in [Testing manifests](guides/testing.md).

## 8. Load it as a real command

So far every call went through `cli run`. Load the manifest to get a `notes` command:

```console
$ cli load notes.yaml
✨ Generated notes CLI v0.1.0 ✨
$ notes -h
$ notes add --help

 Usage: notes add [OPTIONS] {text}

 Add a note

╭─ Arguments ────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────╮
│ *    text      <str>  Text of the note [required]                          │
╰────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────╯
╭─ Options ──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────╮
│ --tag   -t      <str>  Tag to file the note under [default: general]       │
│ --help  -h             Show this message and exit.                         │
╰────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────╯
```

`notes` stays available in this environment until you run `cli remove notes`. After you edit the
manifest, run `cli update notes` to regenerate it, or let [`cli dev`](guides/dev-loop.md) do that
on every save.

## 9. Ship it as one file

```console
$ cli build notes.yaml -o dist
+ notes built 📦
  dist/notes (single file, needs Python >=3.10, 1.8 MB)
  run it with: ./dist/notes
$ ./dist/notes --version
notes, 0.1.0
```

`dist/notes` is a self-contained zipapp. It runs on any machine with a compatible Python 3 and does
not need cliffy. With `--target script` you get a single Python script instead, and with
`--target native` a compiled executable that does not even need Python. More in
[Building executables](guides/building.md).

## The finished manifest

```yaml title="notes.yaml"
name: notes
version: 0.1.0
help: Keep short notes in a JSON file

imports: |
  import json
  import os
  from collections import Counter
  from pathlib import Path

vars:
  default_file: notes.json

functions:
  - |
    def notes_path() -> Path:
        return Path(os.environ.get("NOTES_FILE", "{{ default_file }}"))
  - |
    def load_notes() -> list[dict]:
        path = notes_path()
        return json.loads(path.read_text()) if path.exists() else []
  - |
    def save_notes(notes: list[dict]) -> None:
        notes_path().write_text(json.dumps(notes, indent=2))

types:
  Text: str = typer.Argument(..., help="Text of the note")
  Tag: str = typer.Option("general", "--tag", "-t", help="Tag to file the note under")

commands:
  add:
    help: Add a note
    params:
      - text: Text
      - tag: Tag
    run: |
      notes = load_notes()
      notes.append({"text": text, "tag": tag})
      save_notes(notes)
      print(f"Added note {len(notes)} [{tag}]")

  list|ls:
    help: List notes, optionally filtered by tag
    params:
      - --tag|-t: str = ""
    run: |
      for number, note in enumerate(load_notes(), start=1):
          if not tag or note["tag"] == tag:
              print(f"{number}. [{note['tag']}] {note['text']}")

  remove|rm:
    help: Remove a note by its number
    params:
      - number: int!
    run: |
      notes = load_notes()
      if not 1 <= number <= len(notes):
          print(f"No note {number}")
          raise typer.Exit(code=1)
      notes.pop(number - 1)
      save_notes(notes)
      print(f"Removed note {number}")

  tags:
    help: Work with tags

  tags.list:
    help: Count notes per tag
    run: |
      for tag, count in sorted(Counter(note["tag"] for note in load_notes()).items()):
          print(f"{tag} ({count})")

  tags.rename:
    help: Rename a tag on every note
    params:
      - old: str!
      - new: str!
    run: |
      notes = load_notes()
      for note in notes:
          if note["tag"] == old:
              note["tag"] = new
      save_notes(notes)
      print(f"Renamed {old} to {new}")

  backup:
    help: Copy the notes file next to itself
    run: |
      $ cp f{notes_path()} f{notes_path()}.bak
      print(f"Backed up to {notes_path()}.bak")

tests:
  - $ rm -f notes.json notes.json.bak
  - add "buy milk" --tag home: assert result.output == "Added note 1 [home]\n"
  - add "ship release": assert "Added note 2 [general]" in result.output
  - list: |
      assert "1. [home] buy milk" in result.output
      assert "2. [general] ship release" in result.output
  - ls -t home: assert result_text == "1. [home] buy milk"
  - tags rename general work: assert result.exit_code == 0
  - tags list: assert "work (1)" in result.output
  - backup: assert "Backed up" in result.output
  - remove 9: assert result.exit_code == 1
  - rm 1: assert "Removed note 1" in result.output
  - $ rm -f notes.json notes.json.bak

examples:
  - command: notes add "buy milk" --tag home
    description: Add a note tagged home.
  - command: notes ls --tag home
    description: Show only the notes tagged home.
```

The `examples` section at the end is shown at the end of `notes --help` and is used by
[`cli docs`](guides/generating-docs.md).

- [Manifest basics](guides/manifest-basics.md) explains how a manifest is put together.
- [Params and types](guides/params.md) covers every way to declare a parameter.
- [Command templates and global params](guides/templates-and-global-params.md) shows how to share
  params between commands.

<!-- docs/guides/manifest-basics.md -->

# Manifest basics

A manifest is one YAML file that describes one CLI. This page explains its parts and how cliffy
turns them into Python. For a hands-on introduction, start with the [Quickstart](../quickstart.md).

## The smallest manifest

Three keys are required: `name`, `version` and `commands`.

```yaml title="hello.yaml"
name: hello
version: 0.1.0

commands:
  world: print("hello world")
```

```console
$ cli run hello.yaml world
hello world
```

## Top-level keys

| Key | What it is for | Guide |
|---|---|---|
| `name` | The command people type. | |
| `version` | Printed by `--version`. Must be a string, so write `"1.0"` with quotes. | |
| `help` | Description shown at the top of `--help`. | |
| `commands` | The commands and the code they run. | [Commands, groups and aliases](commands.md) |
| `imports` | Python imports for the generated module. | [below](#imports-and-functions) |
| `functions` | Helper functions shared by all commands. | [below](#imports-and-functions) |
| `vars` | Variables you can reuse across the manifest. | [Vars and Jinja](vars-and-jinja.md) |
| `types` | Named parameter definitions. | [Params and types](params.md) |
| `global_params` | Params added to commands. | [Templates and global params](templates-and-global-params.md) |
| `command_templates` | Reusable params, hooks and settings. | [Templates and global params](templates-and-global-params.md) |
| `includes` | Other manifests to merge in. | [Includes and merging](includes.md) |
| `requires` | Python packages the CLI depends on. | [below](#dependencies) |
| `cli_options` | Options for the CLI application object. | [below](#cli-options) |
| `use_click` | Generate Click code instead of Typer. | [Click and Typer backends](backends.md) |
| `tests` | Commands to run and assertions to check. | [Testing manifests](testing.md) |
| `examples` | Example command lines, shown in `--help` and in generated docs. | [Generating docs](generating-docs.md) |

Keys that cliffy does not know are ignored. The [manifest reference](../reference/manifest.md) lists
every key with its type and default.

## How a manifest becomes Python

cliffy writes a single Python module from the manifest, in this order:

1. `import subprocess`, `import typer` and the lines from `imports`
2. one variable per entry in `vars`
3. the Typer application, with `--version` built in
4. the `functions`
5. one function per command, registered with Typer

Each command's `run` script becomes the body of its function, and its params become the function's
arguments. That is the whole model: anything you can write in a Python function, you can write in
`run`.

To read the generated module for any manifest:

```console
$ cli render hello.yaml
```

The output is the module itself, so `cli render hello.yaml > hello.py` writes a file you can run. The
closing `# Rendered ...` line goes to the error stream and does not end up in that file.

## Imports and functions

```yaml
imports: |
  import json
  from pathlib import Path

functions:
  - |
    def load(path: str) -> dict:
        return json.loads(Path(path).read_text())
  - |
    def branch() -> str:
        out = $ git rev-parse --abbrev-ref HEAD
        return out.decode().strip()
```

`imports` is a block of text or a list of lines. `functions` is a list with one function per item.
`subprocess` and `typer` are always imported, so `typer.Exit`, `typer.confirm` and friends are
available everywhere.

Write `functions` as a list when a function contains [shell lines](shell-commands.md). A single
block of text is also accepted, but `$` lines inside it are not translated.

## Dependencies

List the packages your code imports under `requires`, using the same specifiers as `pip`:

```yaml
requires:
  - tabulate>=0.9.0
  - rich
```

- `cli load`, `cli run`, `cli test` and `cli validate` stop with `missing requirement` when a listed
  package is not installed in the environment cliffy runs in.
- `cli build` downloads the listed packages and bundles them into the executable.

## CLI options

`cli_options` is passed to the Typer application as keyword arguments. Two common settings:

```yaml
cli_options:
  add_completion: false   # hide --install-completion and --show-completion
  no_args_is_help: true   # print help when the CLI is called without a command
```

## Check, run, load

| Command | What it does |
|---|---|
| `cli validate hello.yaml` | Checks the YAML, the schema, the `requires` and that the generated code imports. |
| `cli render hello.yaml` | Prints the generated Python. |
| `cli run hello.yaml -- <args>` | Runs the CLI once without installing it. |
| `cli test hello.yaml` | Runs the `tests` section. |
| `cli load hello.yaml` | Installs the CLI as a command in the current environment. |

All of them are described in the [CLI reference](../reference/cli.md).

## YAML pitfalls

Manifests mix YAML, Jinja and Python, and each has its own special characters.

**A colon followed by a space ends a YAML key.** This one-line command breaks, because of `: ` inside
the string:

```yaml
commands:
  status: print("status: ok")      # YAML error
```

Use a block instead:

```yaml
commands:
  status: |
    print("status: ok")
```

**Quote values that YAML would not read as text.** `version: 1.0` is a number and is rejected;
`version: "1.0"` works. The same applies to values in `vars`.

**Quote a one-line command that starts with `>`.** YAML treats a leading `>` as its own syntax, so
write `run: "> ls *.txt"`.

**Double braces belong to Jinja.** `{{ name }}` is replaced when the manifest is loaded. To get
literal double braces into your Python, see [Vars and Jinja](vars-and-jinja.md#literal-braces).

## Editor support

cliffy publishes a JSON schema for manifests, which gives you completion and validation while you
type. See [Editor setup](editor-setup.md).

<!-- docs/guides/params.md -->

# Params and types

Params are the arguments and options of a command. Inside `run` they are ordinary Python variables.
A `params` list accepts three forms, and you can mix them in one command.

| Form | Looks like | Use it when |
|---|---|---|
| [Shorthand](#shorthand) | `- name: str!` | You want the shortest syntax. |
| [Explicit](#explicit) | `- name: image` and more keys | You want help text. |
| [Generic](#generic) | `- 'path: str = typer.Argument(...)'` | You need the full Typer API for one param. |

To reuse one definition across commands, give it a name under [`types`](#types).

## Shorthand

Each entry is `name: type`.

```yaml
  copy:
    help: Shorthand params
    params:
      - source: str!              # required argument
      - target: str = "out.txt"   # optional argument with a default
      - label: str                # optional argument, None when omitted
      - --count|-c: int = 1       # option with a short alias and a default
      - --force|-f: bool = False  # boolean flag
      - --owner: str!             # required option
      - --dry-run: bool = False   # hyphens become underscores in Python
    run: |
      print(source, target, label, count, force, owner, dry_run)
```

| You write | You get |
|---|---|
| `source: str!` | A required positional argument. |
| `target: str = "out.txt"` | An optional argument with a default. |
| `label: str` | An optional argument that is `None` when omitted. |
| `--count|-c: int = 1` | The option `--count` with the short form `-c`. |
| `--force|-f: bool = False` | A flag. `force` is `True` when `--force` or `-f` is passed. |
| `--owner: str!` | A required option. |
| `--dry-run: bool = False` | An option whose variable is `dry_run`. |

Rules:

- A name that starts with `--` is an option. Anything else is a positional argument.
- `!` after the type makes the param required.
- The text after `=` is a Python expression, so string defaults need quotes: `str = "out.txt"`.
- Hyphens in a name become underscores in the variable.
- Positional arguments are read from the command line in the order you list them, so put required
  ones first.

```console
$ cli run params.yaml -- copy a.txt --owner me
a.txt out.txt None 1 False me False
$ cli run params.yaml -- copy a.txt b.txt c -c 3 -f --owner me --dry-run
a.txt b.txt c 3 True me True
```

!!! note "Boolean options without a short form"
    `--dry-run: bool = False` is generated without explicit option names, so Typer also adds the
    negative form `--no-dry-run`. Options declared with a short form, such as `--force|-f`, get
    only the names you wrote.

## Explicit

Each entry is a mapping. This is the only form with a `help` key.

```yaml
  resize:
    help: Explicit params
    params:
      - name: image
        type: str
        required: true
        help: Image to resize
      - name: --width
        type: int
        default: 800
        short: -w
        help: Target width in pixels
      - name: --format
        type: str
        default: png
        help: Output format
    run: |
      print(image, width, format)
```

| Key | Meaning |
|---|---|
| `name` | Param name. Start it with `--` to make an option; without it the param is a positional argument. |
| `type` | A Python type such as `str`, `int`, `float`, `bool`, or a name from `types`. |
| `default` | Default value. String defaults are quoted for you when `type` is `str`. |
| `help` | Text shown in `--help`. |
| `short` | Short option name including the dash, such as `-w`. Options only. |
| `required` | `true` to make the param required. |

```console
$ cli run params.yaml -- resize cat.jpg -w 100 --format gif
cat.jpg 100 gif
```

## Types

`types` gives a name to a type or to a complete Typer parameter definition. Use the name wherever a
type is expected, in shorthand or explicit params.

```yaml
types:
  Level: int = typer.Option(1, "--level", "-l", min=1, max=5, help="Compression level")
  Source: str = typer.Argument(..., help="File to read")
```

```yaml
  pack:
    help: Params that reuse the types section
    params:
      - source: Source
      - level: Level
    run: |
      print(source, level)
```

A complete definition is everything that follows the param name in a Python signature: the type, then
`typer.Argument(...)` or `typer.Option(...)`. This gives you help text, validation (`min`, `max`),
prompts (`prompt=True`), environment variables (`envvar="NAME"`) and the rest of the
[Typer parameter API](https://typer.tiangolo.com/tutorial/options/). It replaces everything the param
entry says except its name, so a default or `help` written next to it is not used.

A plain type is an alias:

```yaml
types:
  Count: int = 1

commands:
  repeat:
    params:
      - --times: Count       # the option --times, an int, default 1
      - --retries: Count = 3 # a default on the param wins
    run: print(times, retries)
```

The param keeps what its own entry says: `--times` is an option because of its name, and an explicit
param keeps its `help`. Plain types work with both backends.

```console
$ cli run params.yaml -- pack data.csv
data.csv 1
$ cli run params.yaml -- pack data.csv -l 9
╭─ Error ────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────╮
│ Invalid value for '--level' / '-l': 9 is not in the range 1<=x<=5.         │
╰────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────╯
```

## Generic

A plain string is copied into the function signature exactly as written. Quote the whole entry so
that YAML reads it as a string.

```yaml
  tail:
    help: Raw Typer signatures
    params:
      - 'path: str = typer.Argument(..., help="File to follow")'
      - 'lines: int = typer.Option(10, "--lines", "-n", min=1, help="Lines to show")'
    run: |
      print(path, lines)
```

!!! tip "A Typer definition also works in a shorthand entry"
    `- name: str = typer.Option("World", "--name")` is passed through as written. Use `types` when
    several commands share the definition.

## Where else params appear

- `global_params` and `command_templates.<name>.params` accept the same three forms. See
  [Command templates and global params](templates-and-global-params.md).
- With `use_click: true`, params are translated to Click decorators. Shorthand and explicit params
  mean the same; generic params and full definitions in `types` are written as Click decorators. See
  [Click and Typer backends](backends.md).

## The complete example

```yaml title="params.yaml"
name: params
version: 0.1.0
help: One command per way of declaring parameters

types:
  Level: int = typer.Option(1, "--level", "-l", min=1, max=5, help="Compression level")
  Source: str = typer.Argument(..., help="File to read")

commands:
  copy:
    help: Shorthand params
    params:
      - source: str!              # required argument
      - target: str = "out.txt"   # optional argument with a default
      - label: str                # optional argument, None when omitted
      - --count|-c: int = 1       # option with a short alias and a default
      - --force|-f: bool = False  # boolean flag
      - --owner: str!             # required option
      - --dry-run: bool = False   # hyphens become underscores in Python
    run: |
      print(source, target, label, count, force, owner, dry_run)

  resize:
    help: Explicit params
    params:
      - name: image
        type: str
        required: true
        help: Image to resize
      - name: --width
        type: int
        default: 800
        short: -w
        help: Target width in pixels
      - name: --format
        type: str
        default: png
        help: Output format
    run: |
      print(image, width, format)

  pack:
    help: Params that reuse the types section
    params:
      - source: Source
      - level: Level
    run: |
      print(source, level)

  tail:
    help: Raw Typer signatures
    params:
      - 'path: str = typer.Argument(..., help="File to follow")'
      - 'lines: int = typer.Option(10, "--lines", "-n", min=1, help="Lines to show")'
    run: |
      print(path, lines)

tests:
  - copy a.txt --owner me: assert result.output == "a.txt out.txt None 1 False me False\n"
  - copy a.txt b.txt c -c 3 -f --owner me --dry-run: assert result.output == "a.txt b.txt c 3 True me True\n"
  - copy a.txt: assert result.exit_code == 2
  - resize cat.jpg: assert result.output == "cat.jpg 800 png\n"
  - resize cat.jpg -w 100 --format gif: assert result.output == "cat.jpg 100 gif\n"
  - pack data.csv: assert result.output == "data.csv 1\n"
  - pack data.csv -l 9: assert result.exit_code == 2
  - tail app.log: assert result.output == "app.log 10\n"
  - tail app.log -n 2: assert result.output == "app.log 2\n"
```

<!-- docs/guides/commands.md -->

# Commands, groups and aliases

Everything under `commands` becomes a command of your CLI. The key decides where the command lives
and what it is called; the value decides what it does.

The snippets on this page come from one manifest, shown in full [at the end](#the-complete-example).

## Three ways to write a command

```yaml
  # 1. A string: the whole value is the run script
  ping: print("pong")

  # 2. A list: each item is a line of the run script
  status:
    - print("checking...")
    - $ echo "all good"

  # 3. A mapping: the full form
  greet:
    help: Greet a customer
    params:
      - name: str = "friend"
    run: |
      print(f"Welcome, {name}!")
```

Use the short forms for one-liners and the mapping when you need `help`, `params` or anything else.
The keys of the mapping are listed in the [manifest reference](../reference/manifest.md#command).

```console
$ cli run commands.yaml ping
pong
$ cli run commands.yaml greet
Welcome, friend!
```

Command names may contain letters, digits, `-` and `_`.

## Groups

A dot in the key puts the command in a group. Groups are created as needed and can be nested.

```yaml
  # A dot nests a command inside a group: `shop orders list`
  orders.create:
    help: Create an order
    params:
      - item: str!
    run: print(f"created order for {item}")

  orders.ship:
    help: Ship an order
    params:
      - number: int!
    run: print(f"shipped order {number}")

  # Groups nest as deep as you like: `shop stock warehouse count`
  stock.warehouse.count: print("42 items")

  # A command with help and no run script sets the help text of the group
  orders:
    help: Manage customer orders
```

```console
$ cli run commands.yaml orders create book
created order for book
$ cli run commands.yaml stock warehouse count
42 items
$ cli run commands.yaml -- orders --help
...
╭─ Commands ─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────╮
│ create  Create an order                                                    │
│ ship    Ship an order                                                      │
│ list    List all orders                                                    │
╰────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────╯
```

To describe a group, add an entry with the group's name that has `help` and no `run`, like `orders`
above. A name is either a group or a command: if `orders` had a `run` script while `orders.create`
exists, the group would take the name and the script could not be reached.

## Aliases

```yaml
  # `shop customers add` and `shop customers new` run the same code
  customers.add|new:
    help: Add a customer
    params:
      - name: str!
    run: print(f"added {name}")

  # The aliases field does the same without touching the key
  version-info:
    help: Show build details
    aliases: [vi]
    run: print("build 7")
```

- `|` in the key adds aliases to the last part of the name: `customers.add|new` gives
  `customers add` and `customers new`.
- The `aliases` list does the same from inside the command.

Aliases are hidden from `--help`. When a manifest defines aliases in its keys, the CLI gets an
`--aliases` option that lists them:

```console
$ cli run commands.yaml -- --aliases

Command             Aliases
--------            --------
customers.add       new
```

## One command for every group

A key that starts with `(*)` is added to every group. Inside that command, `{(*)}` is replaced with
the group's name, in `help`, `run`, `pre_run`, `post_run` and params.

```yaml
  # (*) adds this command to every group; {(*)} is replaced by the group name
  (*).list:
    help: List all {(*)}
    params:
      - --limit|-l: int = 10
    run: print(f"listing {limit} {(*)}")
```

```console
$ cli run commands.yaml orders list
listing 10 orders
$ cli run commands.yaml -- customers list -l 3
listing 3 customers
```

## Run scripts

`run` is Python. Write it as a block (`run: |`) or as a list of lines. Lines that start with `$` are
shell commands, described in [Shell commands](shell-commands.md).

Two hooks wrap the script. `pre_run` runs before `run` and `post_run` after it, in the same function,
so all three share variables.

```yaml
  deploy:
    help: Deploy the shop
    pre_run: print("1. pre_run")
    run: print("2. run")
    post_run: print("3. post_run")
```

```console
$ cli run commands.yaml deploy
1. pre_run
2. run
3. post_run
```

Hooks are most useful together with [command templates](templates-and-global-params.md), which let
several commands share them.

To stop a command with an exit code, raise `typer.Exit`:

```yaml
run: |
  if not ready:
      print("not ready")
      raise typer.Exit(code=1)
```

## Help text

`help` on a command is shown in the command list and at the top of the command's own `--help`.
Because `run` is the body of a Python function, a docstring on its first line works as well:

```yaml
  about:
    run: |
      """Show what this CLI is for"""
      print("A demo shop")
```

## Command settings

`config` passes extra settings to Typer for one command.

```yaml
  migrate:
    help: Run the old migration tool
    run: print("migrating")
    config:
      deprecated: true
      hidden: true
      epilog: Use `shop deploy` instead.
```

| Key | Effect |
|---|---|
| `hidden` | Leave the command out of `--help`. |
| `deprecated` | Mark the command as deprecated and print a warning when it runs. |
| `epilog` | Text shown at the end of the command's help. |
| `short_help` | Text for the command list, when it should differ from `help`. |
| `no_args_is_help` | Show help when the command is called without arguments. |
| `context_settings` | Click context settings, for example `help_option_names`. |

All keys are in the [manifest reference](../reference/manifest.md#commandconfig).

## The complete example

```yaml title="commands.yaml"
name: shop
version: 0.1.0
help: Groups, aliases and command options

cli_options:
  add_completion: false
  no_args_is_help: true

commands:
  # 1. A string: the whole value is the run script
  ping: print("pong")

  # 2. A list: each item is a line of the run script
  status:
    - print("checking...")
    - $ echo "all good"

  # 3. A mapping: the full form
  greet:
    help: Greet a customer
    params:
      - name: str = "friend"
    run: |
      print(f"Welcome, {name}!")

  # A dot nests a command inside a group: `shop orders list`
  orders.create:
    help: Create an order
    params:
      - item: str!
    run: print(f"created order for {item}")

  orders.ship:
    help: Ship an order
    params:
      - number: int!
    run: print(f"shipped order {number}")

  # Groups nest as deep as you like: `shop stock warehouse count`
  stock.warehouse.count: print("42 items")

  # A command with help and no run script sets the help text of the group
  orders:
    help: Manage customer orders

  # `shop customers add` and `shop customers new` run the same code
  customers.add|new:
    help: Add a customer
    params:
      - name: str!
    run: print(f"added {name}")

  # The aliases field does the same without touching the key
  version-info:
    help: Show build details
    aliases: [vi]
    run: print("build 7")

  # (*) adds this command to every group; {(*)} is replaced by the group name
  (*).list:
    help: List all {(*)}
    params:
      - --limit|-l: int = 10
    run: print(f"listing {limit} {(*)}")

  deploy:
    help: Deploy the shop
    pre_run: print("1. pre_run")
    run: print("2. run")
    post_run: print("3. post_run")

  migrate:
    help: Run the old migration tool
    run: print("migrating")
    config:
      deprecated: true
      hidden: true
      epilog: Use `shop deploy` instead.

  about:
    run: |
      """Show what this CLI is for"""
      print("A demo shop")

tests:
  - ping: assert result.output == "pong\n"
  - greet: assert result.output == "Welcome, friend!\n"
  - orders create book: assert result.output == "created order for book\n"
  - orders ship 7: assert result.output == "shipped order 7\n"
  - stock warehouse count: assert result.output == "42 items\n"
  - orders --help: assert "Manage customer orders" in result.output
  - customers new Ada: assert result.output == "added Ada\n"
  - vi: assert result.output == "build 7\n"
  - orders list: assert result.output == "listing 10 orders\n"
  - customers list -l 3: assert result.output == "listing 3 customers\n"
  - orders list --help: assert "List all orders" in result.output
  - deploy: assert result.output == "1. pre_run\n2. run\n3. post_run\n"
  - migrate: assert "migrating" in result.output
  - --help: assert "migrate" not in result.output
  - about --help: assert "Show what this CLI is for" in result.output
  - --aliases: assert "customers.add" in result.output
```

<!-- docs/guides/templates-and-global-params.md -->

# Command templates and global params

Two features keep a manifest free of repetition. **Global params** add the same params to your
commands. **Command templates** bundle params, hooks and settings under a name that commands opt
into.

## Global params

`global_params` is a list of [params](params.md), in any of the three forms.

```yaml
types:
  Verbose: bool = typer.Option(False, "--verbose", "-v", help="Print extra detail")

global_params:
  - verbose: Verbose
```

The param is passed to the command itself, so it goes after the command name
(`files delete notes.txt --verbose`) and is available in `run` as a normal variable.

Global params are added to every command, whether or not it has params of its own.

## Command templates

A template can hold `params`, `pre_run`, `post_run` and `config`.

```yaml
command_templates:
  destructive:
    params:
      - --yes|-y: bool = False
    pre_run: |
      if not yes:
          typer.confirm("Are you sure?", abort=True)
    post_run: print("done")
    config:
      epilog: This command changes files on disk.
```

A command uses it with `template: <name>`:

```yaml
commands:
  delete|rm:
    help: Delete a file
    template: destructive
    params:
      - path: str!
    pre_run: |
      if verbose:
          print(f"about to delete {path}")
    run: print(f"deleted {path}")
    post_run: print("cleaning up")

  wipe:
    help: Delete everything
    template: destructive
    run: print("wiped")
    config:
      epilog: There is no undo.
```

```console
$ cli run templates.yaml -- delete notes.txt --yes --verbose
about to delete notes.txt
deleted notes.txt
cleaning up
done
$ cli run templates.yaml delete notes.txt
Are you sure? [y/N]: n
Aborted.
```

### How a template is merged into a command

| Part | Result |
|---|---|
| `params` | Template params first, then the command's own. |
| `pre_run` | Template `pre_run`, then the command's. |
| `post_run` | The command's `post_run`, then the template's. |
| `config` | Combined. A key set on the command overrides the same key from the template. |

Together with global params, a command's arguments are ordered: global params, template params,
command params.

The scripts therefore always run in this order:

1. template `pre_run`
2. command `pre_run`
3. command `run`
4. command `post_run`
5. template `post_run`

All five are placed in one function, so a variable set in `pre_run` can be used in `run`.

In the example, `wipe` sets its own `epilog`, which replaces the one from the template, while
`delete` keeps the template's:

```console
$ cli run templates.yaml -- delete --help
...
╭─ Options ──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────╮
│ --verbose  -v        Print extra detail                                    │
│ --yes      -y                                                              │
│ --help     -h        Show this message and exit.                           │
╰────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────╯

 This command changes files on disk.
```

A command can use one template. Naming a template that does not exist is an error when the manifest
is loaded.

## The complete example

```yaml title="templates.yaml"
name: files
version: 0.1.0
help: Command templates and global params

types:
  Verbose: bool = typer.Option(False, "--verbose", "-v", help="Print extra detail")

global_params:
  - verbose: Verbose

command_templates:
  destructive:
    params:
      - --yes|-y: bool = False
    pre_run: |
      if not yes:
          typer.confirm("Are you sure?", abort=True)
    post_run: print("done")
    config:
      epilog: This command changes files on disk.

commands:
  delete|rm:
    help: Delete a file
    template: destructive
    params:
      - path: str!
    pre_run: |
      if verbose:
          print(f"about to delete {path}")
    run: print(f"deleted {path}")
    post_run: print("cleaning up")

  wipe:
    help: Delete everything
    template: destructive
    run: print("wiped")
    config:
      epilog: There is no undo.

tests:
  - delete notes.txt --yes: assert result.output == "deleted notes.txt\ncleaning up\ndone\n"
  - rm notes.txt -y -v: assert result.output == "about to delete notes.txt\ndeleted notes.txt\ncleaning up\ndone\n"
  - wipe -y: assert result.output == "wiped\ndone\n"
  - wipe: assert result.exit_code == 1
  - delete --help: assert "This command changes files on disk." in result.output
  - wipe --help: assert "There is no undo." in result.output
  - wipe --help: assert "--verbose" in result.output
```

<!-- docs/guides/includes.md -->

# Includes and merging

`includes` merges other YAML files into a manifest. Use it to share functions, types and commands
between several CLIs.

## An include file

An include file looks like a manifest without `name` and `version`:

```yaml title="shared/common.yaml"
imports:
  - import json

vars:
  team: platform

functions:
  - |
    def as_json(data: dict) -> str:
        return json.dumps(data, sort_keys=True)

types:
  Service: str = typer.Argument(..., help="Name of the service")

commands:
  health:
    help: Report service health
    params:
      - service: Service
    run: |
      print(as_json({"service": service, "status": "ok"}))

  whoami:
    help: Show the owning team
    run: print(team)

tests:
  - health api: assert '"ok"' in result.output
```

It may contain `commands`, `functions`, `imports`, `types`, `vars`, `requires`, `cli_options` and
`tests`. In an include file, `functions` must be a list.

## Using it

```yaml title="ops.yaml"
name: ops
version: 0.1.0
help: Commands shared between CLIs through includes

includes:
  - shared/common.yaml

commands:
  restart:
    help: Restart a service
    params:
      - service: Service
    run: |
      print(as_json({"service": service, "action": "restart"}))

  # Same key as in the include: the keys set here win, the rest is inherited
  whoami:
    help: Show who owns this CLI

tests:
  - restart api: assert '"restart"' in result.output
  - whoami: assert result.output == "platform\n"
  - whoami --help: assert "Show who owns this CLI" in result.output
```

```console
$ cli run ops.yaml health api
{"service": "api", "status": "ok"}
$ cli run ops.yaml restart api
{"action": "restart", "service": "api"}
$ cli run ops.yaml whoami
platform
```

`restart` is defined in `ops.yaml` and uses the `Service` type and the `as_json` function from the
include. `health` comes entirely from the include.

!!! note "Paths are relative to the manifest"
    `shared/common.yaml` is looked up next to the manifest that includes it first, and in the current
    working directory after that. A manifest that includes itself, directly or through another file,
    is reported as a circular include. `cli dev` watches included files too.

## How files are merged

All included files are merged together first. The result is then merged into your manifest.

| Kind of value | Rule | Example |
|---|---|---|
| Mapping | Merged key by key, at every level. | `commands`, `types`, `vars`, and the keys of a single command |
| List | Items from the include are added, without duplicates. | `requires`, `tests`, `functions` and `imports` when both are lists |
| Anything else | The value in your manifest wins. | a command's `help` or `run` |

In the example, both files define `whoami`. The command keeps its `run` script from the include and
takes `help` from `ops.yaml`.

Two details to keep in mind:

- When the same key holds a list in one file and a block of text in the other, your manifest's value
  is kept and the include's is dropped. Write `imports` as a list in both files if both need imports.
- Include files are merged in the order they are listed. When two of them set the same key to
  different values, the one listed first wins.

## Variables in include files

Each file is rendered on its own. `{{ team }}` works inside `shared/common.yaml`, where `team` is
defined, but not inside `ops.yaml`. The Python variable `team` is available to every command in the
merged CLI, which is why `whoami` can print it. See [Vars and Jinja](vars-and-jinja.md).

<!-- docs/guides/vars-and-jinja.md -->

# Vars and Jinja

A manifest is rendered as a [Jinja2](https://jinja.palletsprojects.com/) template before it is read
as YAML. `vars` supplies the values. Use them for anything you would otherwise repeat: file names,
URLs, defaults.

## Defining vars

```yaml
vars:
  app: shop
  # Jinja expression, evaluated when the manifest is loaded
  region: "{{ env['DEPLOY_REGION'] or 'eu-west-1' }}"
  # A var can build on other vars
  image: "registry.example.com/{{ app }}:{{ region }}"
  # Numbers and booleans keep their type
  retries: 3
  # A value in braces is a Python expression instead of a string
  workdir: {os.getcwd()}
```

There are three kinds of value:

| You write | The var is |
|---|---|
| `app: shop` | The string `shop`. |
| `region: "{{ env['DEPLOY_REGION'] or 'eu-west-1' }}"` | A string computed by a Jinja expression. |
| `image: "registry.example.com/{{ app }}:{{ region }}"` | A string built from other vars. |
| `retries: 3` | The integer `3`. Numbers and booleans keep their type. |
| `workdir: {os.getcwd()}` | The Python expression `os.getcwd()`, evaluated each time the CLI starts. |

Quote a string value that starts with `{{`, and quote a number that should stay text
(`zip_code: "02134"`). Braces around a value turn it into a Python expression.

A var name becomes a Python variable, so it has to be a valid identifier: `data_file`, not
`data-file`. Names the generated code uses itself, such as `cli` and `typer`, are rejected too.

Vars can use each other in any order. cliffy resolves them before the rest of the file, and reports
vars that refer to each other in a circle:

```text
~ error loading manifest: vars.yaml: vars reference each other in a circle: a -> b -> a. A var cannot be built from itself.
```

## Using vars

Every var is available in two ways.

```yaml
  show:
    help: Print the resolved variables
    run: |
      print("app={{ app }} region={{ region }} image={{ image }}")
      print(f"app={app} retries={retries + 1} cwd={workdir == os.getcwd()}")
```

```console
$ cli run vars.yaml show
app=shop region=eu-west-1 image=registry.example.com/shop:eu-west-1
app=shop retries=4 cwd=True
```

1. **As a placeholder.** `{{ app }}` is replaced with the value when the manifest is loaded. This
   works anywhere in the file: in scripts, help text, params, even in command names.
2. **As a Python variable.** The generated module defines `app = 'shop'`, so `run` scripts and
   functions can use `app` directly, and `retries = 3` as a number. A var written with braces, like
   `workdir`, is only useful this way.

A placeholder for a name that is not defined is replaced with nothing, without an error. If output
is unexpectedly empty, check the spelling with `cli render`.

## Environment variables

`env` holds the environment of the process that loads the manifest.

```yaml
vars:
  region: "{{ env['DEPLOY_REGION'] or 'eu-west-1' }}"
```

```console
$ DEPLOY_REGION=us-east-2 cli run vars.yaml show
app=shop region=us-east-2 image=registry.example.com/shop:us-east-2
app=shop retries=4 cwd=True
```

`env` can be used in `vars` and anywhere else in the file.

The value is read **when the manifest is loaded or built** and then fixed in the generated code. A
CLI installed with `cli load` keeps the value it saw at load time. To read the environment each
time a command runs, use Python instead:

```yaml
imports:
  - import os

commands:
  region: print(os.environ.get("DEPLOY_REGION", "eu-west-1"))
```

## Loops and conditions

Jinja statements such as `{% for %}` and `{% if %}` work as long as the file is still valid YAML
before rendering. Put them in YAML comments:

```yaml
  # {% for stage in ['staging', 'production'] %}
  deploy.{{ stage }}:
    help: Deploy {{ app }} to {{ stage }}
    run: print("deploying {{ app }} to {{ stage }} in {{ region }}")
  # {% endfor %}
```

```console
$ cli run vars.yaml deploy staging
deploying shop to staging in eu-west-1
$ cli run vars.yaml deploy production
deploying shop to production in eu-west-1
```

The loop produces one `deploy.<stage>` command per item.

## Literal braces

To keep double braces in your Python code, wrap them in `{% raw %}`:

```yaml
  braces:
    help: Print literal double braces
    run: print({% raw %}"{{ not a variable }}"{% endraw %})
```

Single braces, as used in f-strings (`f"{name}"`), need no escaping.

## Comments are part of the template

The whole file is rendered, YAML comments included. That is what makes the loop above possible, and
it means that double braces in a comment are read as a placeholder too. A comment such as
`# use {{ }} for placeholders` is a Jinja syntax error, which is reported with its line:

```text
~ error loading manifest: vars.yaml, line 12: Jinja syntax error: Expected an expression, got 'end of print statement'
    # use {{ }} for placeholders
  The whole file is a Jinja template, comments included. To keep braces as text, wrap them in {% raw %} and {% endraw %}.
```

Write the comment without double braces, or wrap them in `{% raw %}`.

## Limits

- Vars defined in an [include file](includes.md) can be used as placeholders only inside that file.

## The complete example

```yaml title="vars.yaml"
name: deployer
version: 0.1.0
help: Variables and Jinja templating

imports:
  - import os

vars:
  app: shop
  # Jinja expression, evaluated when the manifest is loaded
  region: "{{ env['DEPLOY_REGION'] or 'eu-west-1' }}"
  # A var can build on other vars
  image: "registry.example.com/{{ app }}:{{ region }}"
  # Numbers and booleans keep their type
  retries: 3
  # A value in braces is a Python expression instead of a string
  workdir: {os.getcwd()}

commands:
  show:
    help: Print the resolved variables
    run: |
      print("app={{ app }} region={{ region }} image={{ image }}")
      print(f"app={app} retries={retries + 1} cwd={workdir == os.getcwd()}")

  # {% for stage in ['staging', 'production'] %}
  deploy.{{ stage }}:
    help: Deploy {{ app }} to {{ stage }}
    run: print("deploying {{ app }} to {{ stage }} in {{ region }}")
  # {% endfor %}

  braces:
    help: Print literal double braces
    run: print({% raw %}"{{ not a variable }}"{% endraw %})

tests:
  - show: |
      assert result.output.splitlines() == [
          "app=shop region=eu-west-1 image=registry.example.com/shop:eu-west-1",
          "app=shop retries=4 cwd=True",
      ]
  - deploy staging: assert result.output == "deploying shop to staging in eu-west-1\n"
  - deploy production --help: assert "Deploy shop to production" in result.output
  - braces: assert "not a variable" in result.output
```

<!-- docs/guides/shell-commands.md -->

# Shell commands

In any script, a line that starts with `$` is run as an external command. cliffy uses
[pybash](https://github.com/jaykv/pybash) to translate these lines into `subprocess` calls, so you
can move between Python and shell freely.

## The basics

```yaml
  hello: $ echo "hello from the shell"

  mixed:
    help: Mix Python and shell lines
    params:
      - name: str!
    run: |
      print("python first")
      $ echo "then shell"
      if name == "ada":
          $ echo "shell lines can be indented"
```

`$ echo "then shell"` becomes `subprocess.run(["echo", "then shell"])`. The command is split into
arguments the way a shell would split it, and is then started directly, without a shell in between.
Shell lines follow Python indentation, so they can sit inside `if` blocks and loops.

`$` lines work in `run`, `pre_run`, `post_run`, in callbacks, in `functions` written as a list, and
as steps in [`tests`](testing.md#shell-steps). Run `cli render` to see the translation.

## Using Python values

`f{expression}` inserts the value of a Python expression into the command. The value is passed as a
single argument, whatever it contains: spaces, quotes and `;` are just text.

```yaml
  say:
    help: Pass a Python value to a shell command
    params:
      - message: str!
    run: $ echo f{message} f{len(message)}
```

```console
$ cli run shell.yaml say "two words"
two words 9
```

Everything an f-string accepts after the expression works too, and `f{ }` can be used inside
quotes:

```yaml
  price:
    help: f{ } takes f-string format specs, also inside quotes
    params:
      - amount: float!
    run: |
      out = $ echo "total: f{amount:,.2f}"
      print(out.decode().strip())
```

### Double braces are Jinja's

pybash also has a `{{ expression }}` form, which inserts `str(expression)`. In a manifest, cliffy
renders [Jinja](vars-and-jinja.md) first, so `{{ name }}` is replaced with a *var* when the manifest
is loaded and never reaches pybash. That is what you want for vars:

```yaml
vars:
  data_file: tasks.json
commands:
  backup: $ cp {{ data_file }} {{ data_file }}.backup
```

For a value that only exists when the command runs, such as a param, use `f{ }`. If you prefer the
double-brace form, put the lines in a Jinja `raw` block so they are left alone:

```yaml
  whoami:
    help: Double braces belong to Jinja unless they are inside a raw block
    params:
      - user: str!
    run: |
      {% raw %}
      out = $ echo {{ user.title() }}
      {% endraw %}
      print(out.decode().strip())
```

To write the markers themselves as text, escape them: `\f{` and, inside a `raw` block, `\{{`.

## Capturing output

Assign a shell line to a variable, or wrap it in parentheses, to get its output as `bytes`.
`$(command)` does the same in the middle of an expression:

```yaml
  upper:
    help: Capture shell output in Python
    run: |
      out = $ echo captured
      print(out.decode().strip().upper())

  inline:
    help: Capture inline with parentheses
    run: print(($ echo inline).decode().strip())

  words:
    help: Capture in the middle of an expression with $( )
    run: print(len($(echo one two three).split()), "words")
```

```console
$ cli run shell.yaml upper
CAPTURED
$ cli run shell.yaml words
3 words
```

A capture that is not wrapped in brackets runs to the end of the line.

## Pipes and redirection

Pipes and redirects are carried out by the generated CLI itself, without a shell:

```yaml
  sorted:
    help: Pipes work without a shell
    run: $ printf 'b\na\n' | sort

  save:
    help: So does redirection
    run: |
      $ echo "saved" > shell-demo.txt
      $ cat shell-demo.txt

  errors-to-file:
    help: Redirect stderr on its own, together with stdout, or into a pipe
    run: |
      $ ls no-such-file 2> shell-demo.txt
      $ ls . no-such-file &> shell-demo.txt
      $ ls . no-such-file > shell-demo.txt 2>&1
      lines = $ ls no-such-file |& wc -l
      print(int(lines), "line of errors")
```

| Operator | Meaning |
|---|---|
| `a | b` | Pipe the output of `a` into `b` |
| `a |& b` | Pipe output and errors |
| `< file` | Read input from a file |
| `> file`, `>> file` | Write or append output |
| `2> file`, `2>> file` | Write or append errors |
| `&> file`, `&>> file` | Write or append both |
| `2>&1`, `>&2` | Send errors to the output, or the output to the errors |

## Chaining commands

`&&` runs the next command when the previous one succeeded, `||` when it failed, and `;` in either
case:

```yaml
  chain:
    help: "&&, || and ; decide what runs next, like in a shell"
    run: |
      out = $ true && echo "first worked" || echo "first failed"
      print(out.decode().strip())
      out = $ false || echo "fallback" ; echo "always"
      print(out.decode().split())
```

Capturing a chain captures the output of every command that ran.

## Long commands and comments

A `$` or `>` line that ends with a backslash continues on the next line. An unquoted `#` starts a
comment that runs to the end of the line:

```yaml
  longest:
    help: "A trailing backslash continues a command, a # starts a comment"
    run: |
      $ printf '%s\n' pear fig banana \
          | sort \
          | tail -n 1 > shell-demo.txt  # the last one in alphabetical order
      $ echo "a # inside quotes is text" >> shell-demo.txt
      print(open("shell-demo.txt").read())
```

A captured command (`out = $ ...`) has to fit on one line.

## When you need a real shell

`$` lines never expand glob patterns (`*.txt`), `~` or environment variables (`$HOME`), and they do
not support background jobs (`&`) or here-documents (`<<`). For those, start the line with `>`
instead of `$`. The line is handed to the shell as written:

```yaml
  texts:
    help: Glob patterns need a real shell
    run: "> ls *.txt"
```

This becomes `subprocess.run("ls *.txt", shell=True)`. A one-line command that starts with `>` must
be quoted, because `>` also has a meaning in YAML.

Values inserted with `f{ }` are quoted for the place they appear in, so a value is always one word
of data and never shell syntax. Here `name` can be `; rm -rf ~` and nothing is removed:

```yaml
  find:
    help: A value in a > line is quoted for the shell
    params:
      - name: str!
    run: |
      > ls | grep -c f{name} || echo "nothing is called" f{name}

  glob:
    help: Splice a value in as shell syntax, here a glob pattern
    params:
      - pattern: str!
    run: |
      {% raw %}
      > ls {{! pattern }}
      {% endraw %}
```

`{{! expression }}` is the exception: it splices the value in unquoted, so that it can be a glob
pattern or several arguments. Like every double-brace form it has to sit in a `raw` block.

!!! danger "Never pass user input to `{{! }}`"
    A spliced value is interpreted by the shell. A parameter value such as `; rm -rf ~` would be
    executed. Use `f{ }` for anything that comes from a user, and prefer `$` lines, which have no
    shell to inject into. See the Python documentation on
    [subprocess security](https://docs.python.org/3/library/subprocess.html#security-considerations).

## Errors

A shell line that fails does not stop the script. Check the result yourself when it matters:

```yaml
  careless:
    help: A failing command does not stop the script
    run: |
      $ false
      print("still running")

  careful:
    help: Check the exit status yourself
    run: |
      result = subprocess.run(["false"])
      if result.returncode != 0:
          print("command failed")
          raise typer.Exit(code=result.returncode)
```

Two exceptions:

- A command that does not exist raises `FileNotFoundError`.
- A captured command (`out = $ ...`) raises `subprocess.CalledProcessError` when it exits with a
  non-zero status.

A shell line that cannot be translated is reported when the manifest is loaded, with the command it
is in, the line and the column:

```console
$ cli load deploy.yaml
~ error in deploy.yaml: command `ship`, run, line 2, column 11: running in the background with & is not supported in a $ command; use a > shell command
    $ sleep 5 &
              ^ 💔
```

## Things to know

- Output of `$` lines goes straight to the terminal. It is not part of `result.output` in
  [manifest tests](testing.md); capture it and `print` it if you want to assert on it.
- A CLI that only uses plain commands imports nothing but `subprocess`. Pipes, redirects, chains and
  values in `>` lines go through a small helper, `pybash.runtime`, which the generated code imports
  as `_pybash`. `cli build` copies that helper into the file it builds, so a built CLI does not need
  pybash.
- Quoting follows POSIX shell rules: single quotes are literal, double quotes allow `\"` and `\\`,
  and a backslash escapes the next character. Quote or escape an operator to pass it as text:
  `$ echo 'a && b' \| c`.

## The complete example

```yaml title="shell.yaml"
name: sh
version: 0.1.0
help: Shell commands in run scripts

functions:
  - |
    def current_branch() -> str:
        out = $ git rev-parse --abbrev-ref HEAD
        return out.decode().strip()

commands:
  hello: $ echo "hello from the shell"

  mixed:
    help: Mix Python and shell lines
    params:
      - name: str!
    run: |
      print("python first")
      $ echo "then shell"
      if name == "ada":
          $ echo "shell lines can be indented"

  say:
    help: Pass a Python value to a shell command
    params:
      - message: str!
    run: $ echo f{message} f{len(message)}

  price:
    help: f{ } takes f-string format specs, also inside quotes
    params:
      - amount: float!
    run: |
      out = $ echo "total: f{amount:,.2f}"
      print(out.decode().strip())

  whoami:
    help: Double braces belong to Jinja unless they are inside a raw block
    params:
      - user: str!
    run: |
      {% raw %}
      out = $ echo {{ user.title() }}
      {% endraw %}
      print(out.decode().strip())

  upper:
    help: Capture shell output in Python
    run: |
      out = $ echo captured
      print(out.decode().strip().upper())

  inline:
    help: Capture inline with parentheses
    run: print(($ echo inline).decode().strip())

  words:
    help: Capture in the middle of an expression with $( )
    run: print(len($(echo one two three).split()), "words")

  sorted:
    help: Pipes work without a shell
    run: $ printf 'b\na\n' | sort

  save:
    help: So does redirection
    run: |
      $ echo "saved" > shell-demo.txt
      $ cat shell-demo.txt

  errors-to-file:
    help: Redirect stderr on its own, together with stdout, or into a pipe
    run: |
      $ ls no-such-file 2> shell-demo.txt
      $ ls . no-such-file &> shell-demo.txt
      $ ls . no-such-file > shell-demo.txt 2>&1
      lines = $ ls no-such-file |& wc -l
      print(int(lines), "line of errors")

  chain:
    help: "&&, || and ; decide what runs next, like in a shell"
    run: |
      out = $ true && echo "first worked" || echo "first failed"
      print(out.decode().strip())
      out = $ false || echo "fallback" ; echo "always"
      print(out.decode().split())

  longest:
    help: "A trailing backslash continues a command, a # starts a comment"
    run: |
      $ printf '%s\n' pear fig banana \
          | sort \
          | tail -n 1 > shell-demo.txt  # the last one in alphabetical order
      $ echo "a # inside quotes is text" >> shell-demo.txt
      print(open("shell-demo.txt").read())

  texts:
    help: Glob patterns need a real shell
    run: "> ls *.txt"

  find:
    help: A value in a > line is quoted for the shell
    params:
      - name: str!
    run: |
      > ls | grep -c f{name} || echo "nothing is called" f{name}

  glob:
    help: Splice a value in as shell syntax, here a glob pattern
    params:
      - pattern: str!
    run: |
      {% raw %}
      > ls {{! pattern }}
      {% endraw %}

  careless:
    help: A failing command does not stop the script
    run: |
      $ false
      print("still running")

  careful:
    help: Check the exit status yourself
    run: |
      result = subprocess.run(["false"])
      if result.returncode != 0:
          print("command failed")
          raise typer.Exit(code=result.returncode)

tests:
  - hello: assert result.exit_code == 0
  - mixed ada: assert "python first" in result.output
  - say hi: assert result.exit_code == 0
  - upper: assert result.output == "CAPTURED\n"
  - inline: assert result.output == "inline\n"
  - words: assert result.output == "3 words\n"
  - price 1234.5: 'assert result.output == "total: 1,234.50\n"'
  - whoami ada: assert result.output == "Ada\n"
  - sorted: assert result.exit_code == 0
  - save: assert result.exit_code == 0
  - errors-to-file: assert result.output == "1 line of errors\n"
  - chain: assert result.output == "first worked\n['fallback', 'always']\n"
  - longest: assert result.output.splitlines()[0] == "pear" and "inside quotes" in result.output
  - find "; echo injected": assert result.exit_code == 0
  - glob "*.yaml": assert result.exit_code == 0
  - texts: assert result.exit_code == 0
  - careless: assert result.output == "still running\n"
  - careful: assert result.exit_code == 1
  - $ rm -f shell-demo.txt
```

<!-- docs/guides/backends.md -->

# Click and Typer backends

cliffy can generate two kinds of code from the same manifest.

| | Typer (default) | Click |
|---|---|---|
| Enable with | nothing | `use_click: true` |
| Generated code uses | `typer` | `rich_click`, or plain `click` when rich-click is not installed |
| Extra install | none | none. `pip install "cliffy[rich]"` adds rich-formatted help |
| Supported manifest features | all | all, with the differences listed below |

**Use Typer unless you have a specific reason to generate Click code.** Typer is the backend the rest
of this documentation describes.

## The Click backend

```yaml title="click.yaml"
name: clicky
version: 0.1.0
help: The same manifest format, rendered with Click
use_click: true

commands:
  hello|hi:
    help: Say hello
    params:
      - name: str!
      - --times: int = 1
    run: |
      for _ in range(times):
          print(f"hello {name}")

  resize:
    help: Explicit params work like in Typer
    params:
      - name: image
        type: str
        required: true
        help: File to resize
      - name: --width
        type: int
        short: -w
        default: 800
        help: Target width
    run: print(image, width)

  tag:
    help: Raw Click decorators
    params:
      - "@click.option('--loud', is_flag=True, help='Shout the tags')"
      - "@click.argument('tags', nargs=-1)"
    run: |
      for tag in tags:
          print(tag.upper() if loud else tag)

  db.migrate:
    help: Groups work the same way
    run: $ echo "migrating"

tests:
  - hello Ada --times 2: assert result.output == "hello Ada\nhello Ada\n"
  - hi Ada: assert result.output == "hello Ada\n"
  - resize cat.jpg -w 100: assert result.output == "cat.jpg 100\n"
  - resize: assert result.exit_code == 2
  - tag --loud a b: assert result.output == "A\nB\n"
  - db migrate: assert result.exit_code == 0
```

```console
$ cli run click.yaml -- hello Ada --times 2
hello Ada
hello Ada
$ cli run click.yaml -- resize cat.jpg -w 100
cat.jpg 100
$ cli run click.yaml -- tag --loud a b
A
B
$ cli run click.yaml db migrate
migrating
```

### What works

- Commands, groups (`db.migrate`) and aliases (`hello|hi`)
- Shorthand and explicit params with the same meaning as for Typer: a name with `--` is an option,
  anything else is a positional argument, `!` or `required: true` makes it required, and `short`,
  `default` and `help` are passed on
- `types`, command `config`, `global_params`, `callbacks`, `pre_run`, `post_run` and command templates
- Generic params, written as Click decorators
- `vars`, `imports`, `functions`, `includes`, shell lines and `cli test`

### What differs from Typer

| Feature | With `use_click: true` |
|---|---|
| Generic params | A string param is a Click decorator such as `"@click.option('--loud', is_flag=True)"`. A Typer signature entry is rejected. |
| `types` | A plain type (`Count: int`, `Count: int = 1`) works with both backends. A full definition is a Click decorator, `Loud: "@click.option('--loud', is_flag=True)"`; a `typer.Option(...)` definition is rejected with an error that names the command. |
| Inline `typer.Option(...)` in a shorthand param | Rejected. Use a Click decorator. |
| List types | `--tag: list[str]` can be given several times and arrives as a tuple, not a list. |
| Boolean options | `--loud: bool = False` is a `--loud/--no-loud` switch, also when it has a short form. |
| `config.rich_help_panel` | Passed to rich-click as `panel`. The generated code then requires rich-click. |
| `--version` output | `<program>, version <version>` instead of `<name>, <version>`. |

A manifest that uses something the Click backend cannot express stops with an error such as:

```text
~ error in tools.yaml: command `pack`: param `level` uses types.Level, which is a Typer definition (...)
```

### rich-click is optional

The generated module starts with:

```python
try:
    import rich_click as click
except ImportError:  # plain help output when rich-click is not installed
    import click
```

With rich-click installed the help is formatted with Rich. Without it the same CLI runs on plain
Click, which cliffy always installs. `cli build` reads this import and ships rich-click with the
built CLI.

### Building

`cli build` reads the import of `rich_click` from the generated code and bundles rich-click instead of
Typer, so the manifest does not have to list it under `requires`.

## Typer notes

- Typer depends on Rich, so generated CLIs print styled help and tracebacks without extra setup.
- Typer adds `--install-completion` and `--show-completion` to every CLI. Turn them off with:

    ```yaml
    cli_options:
      add_completion: false
    ```

- Anything from the [Typer documentation](https://typer.tiangolo.com/) that fits in a function
  signature or body can be used in `types`, generic params and `run` scripts.

<!-- docs/guides/testing.md -->

# Testing manifests

A manifest can carry its own tests. Each test runs a command of your CLI and checks the result with
Python assertions. `cli test` runs them without loading or building anything.

## Writing tests

```yaml
tests:
  # A string starting with $ or > is a shell step, handy for setup and cleanup
  - $ rm -f counter.txt

  # A mapping is a test case: the command line, then the assertion to run
  - show: assert result.output == "0\n"
  - bump: assert result.exit_code == 0

  # Use a block when you need several statements
  - bump --by 2: |
      assert result.exit_code == 0
      assert result_text == "3"

  # Usage errors exit with code 2
  - bump --by nope: assert result.exit_code == 2

  # An uncaught exception is stored on the result
  - crash: |
      assert result.exit_code == 1
      assert isinstance(result.exception, ValueError)

  - "> rm -f counter.*"
```

```console
$ cli test testing.yaml
✨ Invoking tests ✨

🪄 > counter show

⚗️ >
0


✅ 1 of 5

...

💚 All tests passed!
```

### Test cases

A test case is a one-key mapping:

```yaml
- <command line>: <assertion code>
```

The command line is everything you would type after the CLI's name. It is split like a shell would
split it, so quotes work: `add "buy milk" --tag home`.

The assertion code is Python. Two variables are available:

| Variable | What it is |
|---|---|
| `result` | The outcome of the command. Use `result.output` (everything the command printed), `result.exit_code` and `result.exception`. |
| `result_text` | `result.output` with leading and trailing whitespace removed. |

Use `assert` statements. A test passes when the code runs without raising.

### Shell steps

An entry that is a plain string is a setup or cleanup step, not a test case. It must start with `$`
or `>` and follows the rules of [shell commands](shell-commands.md): `$` runs the command directly,
`>` runs it through a shell (needed for glob patterns such as `counter.*`). Quote an entry that
starts with `>`.

Entries run from top to bottom, so order the steps and cases accordingly.

## Running tests

```console
$ cli test testing.yaml
$ cli test testing.yaml --exitfirst
```

`--exitfirst` (or `-x`) stops at the first failing test.

A failing assertion is reported with its line:

```text
💔 AssertionError: (line 1) > assert result.output == "1\n"
```

So is an assertion that raises something else, or that is not valid Python:

```text
💔 NameError: name 'reslt' is not defined (line 1) > assert reslt.exit_code == 0
```

When the command itself raises, the exception is reported against the manifest: the command, the
exception, and the line of the `run`, `pre_run` or `post_run` block it was raised on.

```text
💥 command `add` raised KeyError: 'notes'
    run, line 2: data["notes"].append(text)
```

No Python traceback is printed. The assertions still run, so a test can expect the exception with
`assert isinstance(result.exception, KeyError)`. To see the full traceback of the command as well:

```console
$ cli test testing.yaml --traceback
```

The run ends with one of three messages:

| Last line | Meaning | Exit code |
|---|---|---|
| `💚 All tests passed!` | Every test case passed. | 0 |
| `💛 Some tests failed :(` | At least one passed and at least one failed. | 1 |
| `All tests failed 💔` | No test case passed. | 1 |

The exit code is 0 only when every test case passed, so a CI job can run `cli test mycli.yaml` as a
step of its own.

## Things to know

- **Colors and styles are removed from the output** before your assertions run, so a test gives the
  same result in a terminal and on a CI system.
- **Tests run in the current directory** and are not isolated from each other. A command that
  writes a file really writes it. Clean up with shell steps, as the example does.
- **Output of `$` lines is not captured.** It goes to the terminal and is not in `result.output`.
  Assert on the exit code, or capture the output in Python and `print` it. See
  [Shell commands](shell-commands.md#capturing-output).
- **Keep `: ` out of one-line assertions.** YAML reads a colon followed by a space as the end of a
  key, so `- show: assert result.output == "count: 0\n"` is a YAML error. Use a block:

    ```yaml
    - show: |
        assert result.output == "count: 0\n"
    ```

- **The counter counts test cases.** `✅ 2 of 5` is the second test case of five. Shell steps are run
  but not counted, and a failed case keeps its number.
- **Shell steps are not checked.** A step that exits with an error does not fail the run. Assert on
  the state it should have produced in the next test case. A step whose program cannot be started at
  all (it does not exist) ends the run with an error.

## The complete example

```yaml title="testing.yaml"
name: counter
version: 0.1.0
help: A counter stored in a file, with tests

imports: |
  from pathlib import Path

functions:
  - |
    def read_count() -> int:
        path = Path("counter.txt")
        return int(path.read_text()) if path.exists() else 0

commands:
  show:
    help: Print the counter
    run: print(read_count())

  bump:
    help: Increase the counter
    params:
      - --by: int = 1
    run: |
      total = read_count() + by
      Path("counter.txt").write_text(str(total))
      print(total)

  crash:
    help: Always fails
    run: raise ValueError("boom")

tests:
  # A string starting with $ or > is a shell step, handy for setup and cleanup
  - $ rm -f counter.txt

  # A mapping is a test case: the command line, then the assertion to run
  - show: assert result.output == "0\n"
  - bump: assert result.exit_code == 0
```
